fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Adam Stevens, aka Mr. Permie Bear, joins InnerVerse to talk about his exodus to Beartaria, how he left the world of banking and finance behind to start minting a new currency, through the infinite abundance of seeds. As one the men behind Grateful Harvest Seed Company, Adam now provides his rural Missouri community with ancient kernels of life-giving magic, with endless return on investment. We'll also discuss the need for authentic community as society diverges into parallel heaven and hell systems, healthy soil tactics, the wealth of family, and much more.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Pests as Messengers of Imbalance", "body": "Adam explains that pests arrive because plants stressed by incomplete photosynthesis form simple sugars instead of long-chain complex ones, sending out an energetic flag he compares to setting out a big pack of gummy worms, and he suggests the same pattern holds inside the human body. He admits his own Missouri farm still battles bugs. Chance frames the lesson as the core choice between victimhood and responsibility, tying poverty to victimhood in the field and in life, while Adam adds that real responsibility means digging into the whys behind the symptoms rather than asking what to spray."}, {"title": "Reading Soil With Your Own Senses", "body": "Asked how a backyard gardener can know whether soil is good, Adam says a quality microscope is the real superpower. Until then he observes tilth that holds together and then crumbles, visible aggregates, moisture retention, mycelium, arthropods, smell, color, and an old rule of at least 13 worms per cubic foot. He cautions that lab and extension soil tests burn samples down to salts, so they report minerals like cobalt and manganese but miss the biology and how available those nutrients really are. He suggests handling soil in an old growth forest or healthy prairie, then comparing your own."}, {"title": "Why Home Saved Seed Wins", "body": "Adam urges every gardener to save seed, since seed from your best plants in your own conditions carries that information forward and grows better the next year. Lettuce, beans, peas and tomatoes are easy starting points. He argues that big contract farms producing a thousand pounds of tomato seed cannot match a careful home grower, and admits Grateful Harvest does not yet grow all of its 230 varieties. He has tried putting seeds in his mouth before planting without measurable results, warns that amaranth and quinoa are a pain to process, and is waiting to plant 25 pounds of Red Fife wheat."}, {"title": "Rare Tomatoes and Seeds That Find Their Way Home", "body": "Adam's favorite is the Jerusalem tomato a Missouri neighbor recommended, which gave him a two pound, four ounce fruit this year. The Giant Crimson was thought extinct for 80 years until M.I. Gardner planted a handful of seed packs, nursed a single survivor, and revived the line, and Grateful Harvest became the second company to sell it. Adam and his wife once catalogued 450 varieties in a banker's spreadsheet, which became the company when seed got hard to buy. At this year's festival people handed him family zinnias and marigolds, an Italian cucumber, a nearly extinct field pea, and a mystery seed."}, {"title": "Showing Up for the Beartaria Community", "body": "Chance describes the bear community as a parallel society with the high trust to keep going if the wider system falls apart, and offers his own realization that Owen Benjamin acts less like a cult leader than a bouncer who screens out the thin skinned. Adam agrees and adds that resilience comes from being people who take action. He became a behind the scenes fixer for the festival, building showers, planning, and raising Beartaria Beef, rooted in a promise to be the friend he never had time to be as a lender. Chance closes on men stepping up as providers."}]
